Exchange rate stability foreign exchange rate stability

The value of a country's currency remaining constant over time against other countries' currencies, or changing at a low and predictable rate.

Exchange Rate Regimes Exchange Rate Regimes

Today, owing to the importance they carry, particularly for small and open economies, and their potential to directly affect the real economy, exchange rates are used directly as target, indicator or instrument within the framework of the monetary policy implemented. Exchange rate practices take shape between two regimes: the fixed exchange rate regime at one end and free floating at the other. Under a fixed exchange rate regime, the value of the national currency is pegged against a foreign currency or a basket of currencies, and the maintenance of this value is guaranteed by the monetary authority, sometimes explicitly and sometimes implicitly. In Currency Board-type arrangements, while the rate is pegged on the one hand, on the other hand the national money supply is tied entirely to the foreign currency purchases and sales conducted at this rate. Under a free floating exchange rate regime, the price of the exchange rate is determined according to the supply and demand forming in the market. Besides these, many intermediate regimes exist. For example, under a floating regime the rate is largely determined by market supply and demand conditions, but the monetary authority intervenes in the market rarely and in limited amounts; under a managed float regime, again there is no exchange rate target, but interventions can occur frequently for various reasons. Under regimes known as the crawling peg, the rate is guided according to a set of criteria and is intervened in by the monetary authority when necessary. The choice of such exchange rate regimes varies according to the conditions countries find themselves in.

Foreign exchange market foreign exchange market

The physical or virtual environment where the currencies of different countries are bought and sold, and where exchange rates are determined in this process.

Foreign exchange market equilibrium foreign exchange market equilibrium

The situation in which, in a given period, the quantity of foreign currency demanded in the market equals the quantity supplied.

Foreign exchange demand foreign exchange demand

Or in short DE: the total quantity of foreign currency that all units in the economy want to purchase, depending on the exchange rate, in a given period.

Foreign exchange demand curve foreign exchange demand curve

A graphical tool showing the relationship between the exchange rate and the quantity of foreign currency demanded, all else being constant.

World Bank World Bank

An international organization established after 1944 under the name 'International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)' for the reconstruction of Europe. It mainly provides long-term project credits to developing countries. In recent years, the concepts of developing countries' external debts and the fight against poverty have also entered its mandate.

Budget of Regulatory and Supervisory Institutions Regulatory and Supervisory Institutions Budget

; It is the budget of institutions established by special laws such as the Capital Markets Board, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, and the Radio and Television Supreme Council.

Level level of employment istihdam

The level of development determined by taking into account the economic, social, cultural, etc. criteria of a country, province or district. Start-up: the name given to innovative and risky ventures with rapid growth potential.

Low unemployment low unemployment

The low rate of unemployment — defined as persons who are seeking work but are not employed — within the labor force of a country.

Low good inferior good

Products whose demand in the market decreases when the average income level rises.

External debt external debt

The total amount of debt the state has received from households and firms resident abroad, or from other states.

External world rest of the world

All the other countries with which an economy trades and establishes economic relations.

Foreign Trade Balance Foreign Trade Balance

Expresses the difference between the amounts of goods exports and imports carried out between persons resident domestically and persons resident abroad, passing through customs. If exports exceed imports, a foreign trade surplus forms; in the opposite case, a foreign trade deficit forms.

Terms of Trade Terms of Trade

The ratio of the export unit value index to the import unit value index. The terms of trade being above 100 shows that the export prices of the goods subject to foreign trade are higher than their import prices. Unit value indices are calculated by TUIK.

External Dependency External Dependency

In countries that fall short of establishing their own technology and industrial infrastructure, the meeting of the investment goods, raw materials or intermediate goods required for production by importing them from other countries; the inability to produce the said materials and raw materials domestically.

Crowding out effect crowding out effect

The situation of the state's consumption and investment expenditures taking the place of private consumption and investments.

Excludability excludability

Or excludability in consumption: the possibility of preventing persons who have not purchased a good or service from using that good or service.

Externality externality

The effect an economic activity has on persons who are not party to that activity.

Internalizing externalities internalizing externalities

The methods that will ensure that economic units take social costs and benefits into account when making choices.

E

E-Export

The fulfillment of the shipment as Micro Export, by issuing an invoice (VAT-free) on behalf of the individual customer for a foreign-addressed order received through the e-commerce/online (internet) sales channel. E-Commerce: the conducting of commerce online in the digital environment. E-TUYS: the Electronic Incentive Application and Foreign Capital Information System, a web-based application in which the affairs and transactions relating to the investment incentive certificate, managed by the Directorate General for Incentive Implementation and Foreign Capital, are carried out.

Economies of Scope

If the cost of producing two products together is smaller than the sum of the cost of a firm producing only product x and the cost of a firm producing only product y, the existence of economies of scope is spoken of.

Exotic Options Exotic Options

Options shaped according to the demander's needs. Examples of this type are options under the name 'barrier option' that lose their validity if, for instance, the price foreseen in the option for the underlying instrument is passed, or options under the name 'lookback options' that take, for example, the highest price realized in a certain period as the option's price.

Economy economics

Or by its other name economics: the branch of science researching how individuals and societies use the limited resources at their disposal to meet their broad wants and needs.

Economic unit economic unit

; Each decision-making member of households, firms, the government, and the outside world, which constitute the four basic components of the economy.

Economic growth economic growth

The general and permanent increase over time in the quantity of goods and services produced in a country.

Economic fluctuation economic fluctuation

Or the business cycle: the ups and downs seen in total production, income and expenditures within periods of a few years in market economies.

Economic contraction economic contraction

A period in which total production in an economy shows a general decline.

Economic efficiency economic efficiency

Deciding, with limited resources, which products will be produced, how, and for whom, in a way that maximizes the social gain.

economic surplus economic surplus

The total gain the market provides to buyers and sellers, equal to the sum of consumer surplus and producer surplus.

economic expansion economic expansion

A period in which total production in an economy shows a general increase.

Economic Confidence Index Economic Confidence Index

An index summarizing consumers' and producers' assessments, expectations and tendencies regarding the general economic situation, formed by weighting and combining the consumer confidence indicator with the confidence indicators for manufacturing industry (real sector), services, retail trade and construction, adjusted for seasonal effects.

economic profit economic profit

The profit calculation that takes into account both explicit and implicit expenses.

economic globalization economic globalization

; the free movement of goods, services, capital, information, technology, and people across borders.

economic system economic system

The concept describing how economic decisions are taken in a society or region, and the institutional structure relating to this.

ecosystem

Refers to the environment in which interrelated groups sharing a particular place, sector or theme bring together the elements that support and facilitate their business ideas.

incomplete information incomplete information

; the situation where not all relevant parties have all the information that could affect an economic activity, such as price, quality, quantity, or production method.

underemployed underemployed

Persons who cannot work enough in a paid job, or who cannot fully use their knowledge and skills.

Imperfect competition imperfect competition

A market structure lacking all the properties required for ideal competitive conditions.

Disposition effect Disposition effect

The tendency to sell winning positions early and hold losing ones; the behavioral consequence of the pain of realizing losses (loss aversion).

Electronic Funds Transfer System - EFT Electronic Funds Transfer System - EFT

The payment system providing the real-time electronic settlement of payment transactions made in Turkish lira. The owner and operator of the EFT system is the CBRT. The EFT System has two components: the Interbank TL Transfer System and the Customer Funds Transfer System. The EFT System operates between 08:00 and 17:30 every weekday except official holidays, and on half working days the system closes at 13:00.

Electronic Securities Transfer System - ESTS Electronic Securities Transfer System - ESTS

The securities settlement system enabling the transfer and settlement of securities among banks electronically, in real time and on a book-entry basis. In the EMKT System, transactions relating to government domestic debt securities and securities issued by some public institutions are carried out. In the transactions made in the EMKT System, the delivery versus payment (DVP) principle applies. Under this principle, the transfer of securities is made simultaneously with the realization of the fund transfer relating to the said securities. The EMKT System operates between 08:00 and 17:30 every weekday except official holidays, and on half working days the system closes at 13:00. The owner and operator of the EMKT System is the CBRT.

Electronic Money Electronic Money

A monetary value issued in return for funds accepted by the electronic money issuing institution, stored electronically, used to carry out the payment transactions defined in Law No. 6493 on Payment and Securities Settlement Systems, Payment Services and Electronic Money Institutions, and accepted as a means of payment also by real and legal persons other than the electronic money issuing institution.

Electronic Money Institution Electronic Money Institution

The legal person authorized to issue electronic money under Law No. 6493 on Payment and Securities Settlement Systems, Payment Services and Electronic Money Institutions.

Labor labor

Or in short L: the fundamental production factor denoting the physical or mental work and labor performed by people.

Labor supply curve labor supply curve

A graphical tool showing the relationship between the wage level and the quantity of labor supplied, all else being constant.

Excess labor supply excess labor supply

Or unemployment: the situation in which the quantity of labor supplied in the labor market exceeds the quantity demanded.

Labor supply labor supply

Or in short SL: the quantity of labor that households offer to the market, depending on different wage rates, in a given period.

Emek kıtlığı labor shortage

Or excess labor demand: the situation in which the quantity of labor demanded in the labor market exceeds the quantity supplied.

Emek piyasası labor market

Or the labor market: the physical or virtual environment where those who supply labor and those who demand labor come together, and in this process the wage rate of labor is determined.

Emek piyasası dengesi labor market equilibrium

The situation in which, in a given period, the quantity of labor demanded in the market equals the quantity of labor supplied.

Emek talebi labor demand

Or in short DL: the quantity of labor that producers want to employ, depending on different wage rates, in a given period.

Emek talep fazlası excess labor demand

Or labor shortage: the situation in which the quantity of labor demanded in the labor market exceeds the quantity supplied.

Emek verimliliği labor productivity

The average quantity of output per worker in a given period.

Emeğin marjinal ürün değeri marginal value product of labor

Or in short MVPL: the revenue obtained from the sale of the additional product brought by increasing the quantity of labor by one unit.

Emeğin marjinal ürün geliri marginal revenue product of labor

Or in short MRPL: the change seen in total revenue when the quantity of labor is increased by one unit.

Emeğin marjinal ürünü marginal product of labor

Or in short MPL: the change seen in the total quantity of product when the quantity of labor is increased by one unit.

Emeğin ortalama ürünü average product of labor

Or in short APL: the quantity of product produced per unit of labor in a given period.

Emeğin ücret oranı wage rate of labor

Or in short PL: the payment made for using one unit of labor in production.

Emisyon Issue

Putting into circulation, issuing.

Emisyon Grubu Emission Group

The banknote series put into circulation within a particular graphic design approach and size arrangement.

Emisyon Hacmi Value of Banknotes in Circulation

The total of the banknotes issued into circulation by the CBRT and in circulation, together with the banknotes that have been withdrawn from circulation but whose 10-year limitation period has not yet expired and that are found in circulation.

Endeksleme indexation

The correction of monetary quantities at certain intervals and automatically according to a price index, by law or by contract.

Enflasyon Inflation

The tendency of the general price level to rise continuously. Inflation is measured by the official indices published by TUIK (Turkish Statistical Institute) that track consumer and producer price developments.

Örnek: Enflasyon, paranın satın alma gücünü azaltır. ( Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money.)

İngilizce tanım: A general rise in the price level.

Enflasyon Beklentileri Inflation Expectations

Refers to the projections of economic units regarding inflation that has not yet materialized (will occur in the future). To measure inflation expectations, indices derived from various market instruments or surveys such as the Survey of Expectations published by the CBRT can be used.

Enflasyon Hedefi Inflation Target

The annual CPI increase rate set by the CBRT and the Government for three-year periods. The inflation target is defined as the annual inflation in December of each year.

Enflasyon Hedeflemesi Inflation Targeting

Central banks' targeting, generally together with governments, of a specific inflation figure as the aim of monetary policy. In such a practice, it is envisaged that the targeted inflation, to the extent it can affect expectations, will serve as the nominal anchor. Its difference from other policies is the clear announcement of the inflation target to the public and the taking of direct responsibility in this matter. In practice, as the implementing institution, central banks acquire instrument independence directed toward the aim; in other words, central banks can use exchange rate and interest rate policies as they wish with the aim of bringing inflation under control. Such practices can also emerge as a necessity as a result of all the magnitudes in an economy losing their nominal anchor property. For the success of such a policy, elements such as a strong and healthy fiscal structure, an observable and stable relationship between inflation and monetary policy instruments, credibility, independence, accountability and transparency are counted as prerequisites.

Inflation Risk Premium Inflation Risk Premium

Refers to the risk premium added to the real interest rate to compensate for the loss that would occur if inflation materialized above the expected level. In other words, the nominal interest rate contains the real interest rate, inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium. This risk premium arises in countries where inflation fluctuations and uncertainties are present.

Inflation Forecast Inflation Forecast

The medium-term inflation forecasts updated by the CBRT every three months within the framework of current data, models and analyses. While the inflation target announced in advance for a certain period is fixed, the inflation forecast is regularly reviewed in the light of new information.

Inflation Compensation Inflation Compensation

The magnitude that investors demand in order not to suffer real losses, equal to the sum of the inflation expectation and the inflation risk premium.

Inflation Tax Inflation Tax

When money is considered a liability for the institution issuing it into circulation and an asset for the institutions and individuals demanding and holding it, inflation reduces the issuing institution's liability and the holding institution's asset in real terms. In this sense, inflation carries the property of a tax for the earner, and hence, like a tax, causes a transfer of purchasing power.

Inflation Indexed Securities Inflation Indexed Securities

Bonds whose principal and interest payments are linked to a certain price index and which therefore do not suffer a real loss of value. Because the real return of these bonds does not fluctuate despite changes in inflation, offering investors a predictable net return, these bonds are preferred by risk-averse investors.

nonaccelerating inflation rate of unemployment nonaccelerating inflation rate of unemployment

Or by its widely known short name NAIRU: the unemployment rate that keeps a country's labor market in long-run equilibrium and therefore does not lead to an increase in inflation.

Engel curve Engel curve

Or the income-consumption curve: a graphical tool showing the relationship between the consumer's income and the quantity demanded of a certain good, all else being constant.

Engel's Law Engel's Law

The analysis stating that as the income level rises, the share of food expenditures within income will decline.

Early Redemption Early Redemption

The repayment of the principal of a debt before its maturity, together with the interest accrued on it.

Flexible relationship elastic relationship

A one percent increase in one variable resulting in a response of more than one percent in the other variable.

inelastic relationship inelastic relationship

Or a rigid relationship: a one percent increase in one variable resulting in a response of less than one percent in the other variable.

Elasticity elasticity

Or in short ε: the measurement describing by what percentage the variable shown on the vertical axis increases or decreases as a result of a one percent increase in the variable shown on the horizontal axis.

Essential Facilities Doctrine

An asset/facility/infrastructure without which a rival or customer cannot continue its activities by making use of it.

Impact

The social, economic and environmental changes that occur generally within 3-5 years following the completion of a project, positive or negative, expected or unexpected, appearing directly or indirectly.

Impact lag impact lag

The period between the implementation of an economic policy and the effects of that policy being felt.

Efficient Market Hypothesis Efficient Market Hypothesis

This hypothesis predicts that the current prices of instruments traded in a market reflect all the obtainable information relating to those instruments. With the assumption that price is determined by buyers and sellers, the hypothesis assumes that traders can access all attainable information simultaneously and symmetrically. It is predicted that the price formed in this case is the equilibrium price.

Euro Dollar Eurodollar

Used to refer to US dollar deposits held at banks outside the United States or at the foreign branches of US banks. The expression 'Euro' stems from the fact that the great majority of such deposits are held particularly at banks in Western European countries. US dollar accounts held in Asia and all other similar countries are also referred to by this name.

Eurobond Eurobond

Securities issued by the issuing country or institution in a currency other than its own national currency.

Exclusionary Agreements

Agreements made among undertakings with the aim of preventing or obstructing the activities of rivals.

Exemption

Regulated in Article 13 of the Competition Act. The exemption granted to agreements, concerted practices and decisions of undertaking associations, provided the conditions listed in Article 5 of the Act are satisfied, is not absolute.

Eximbank

In our country, the institution that supports and encourages, by supporting the development of exports, the diversification of exported goods and services, the provision of new markets for exported goods, the increase of exporters' shares in international trade, the provision of the necessary support for exporters' ventures, and the provision of competitive strength and assurance to exporters and to contractors and investors operating abroad in international markets, as well as investments to be made abroad and the production and sale of investment goods aimed at export

Explicit Collusion

The attainment of an explicit understanding among rival undertakings on matters such as the setting of price and production quantity, and the sharing of markets and customers.

Exploitative Practices

Some of the cases evaluated under Article 6 of the Competition Act are characterized as exploitative abuse. These are pricing or other practices causing a direct loss in consumer welfare. In such abuses, the dominant undertaking uses the advantage of its market power with the aim of extracting rent from consumers in a way a non-dominant undertaking could not. Excessive pricing and applying unfair trading conditions are among these cases.

Export Cartel

Undertakings operating in the same country acting together to sell or market their products in external markets, thereby obtaining an advantage against their international rivals. This can emerge in forms such as export prices being set jointly by rival undertakings, the sharing of customers, decisions on whether products are to be sold to certain regions via patent or license — that is, the conduct of an export restricted relative to what would occur in a free trade environment

Externalities

Externality refers to the situations in which the production or consumption of goods and services brings a cost (negative externality) or a benefit (positive externality) to other persons. Externalities, which are one of the market failures and create inefficiency, may not be reflected in the prices of the goods and services offered. Pollution is a clear example of a negative externality, also called external diseconomy. Chemical wastes dumped into a lake by an industrial facility, killing the fish and plants in the lake,

slope slope

Or in short μ: the measurement describing by how many units the variable shown on the vertical axis increases or decreases as a result of a one-unit increase in the variable shown on the horizontal axis.

Training Program

The training program that those wishing to benefit from the supports KOSGEB offers to entrepreneurs who want to establish their own business are required to attend beforehand.

Co-financing

The cash contribution committed to being provided by the grant beneficiary, to be spent in the supported project or activity.

Isocost line isocost line

A graphical tool showing the combinations of production factors that can be purchased with the same fixed expenditure.

Isoquant curve isoquant curve

A graphical tool showing the input combinations yielding the same total product, all else being constant.

Isoquant map isoquant map

The whole of the multiple isoquant curves showing different total product quantities.

F

Operating profit operating profit

The situation in which the revenue obtained from production can fully cover the variable expenses arising from production.

Operating loss operating loss

The situation in which the revenue obtained from production cannot fully cover the variable expenses arising from production.

Failing Firm

The firm that is continuously loss-making, to the point where the liquidation of its business becomes likely, and is losing market share.

Failing Firm Defense

Mergers and acquisitions resulting in a substantial restriction of competition can, in some special cases, be permitted on the basis of economic and rational justifications; the failing firm defense constitutes one of these special cases.

Interest interest

The predetermined payment made in return for using capital belonging to someone else.

Example: Interest expense is accounted for using the effective interest method.( Interest expense is recognised using the effective interest method.

İngilizce tanım: The cost of using borrowed money.

Faiz dışı bütçe dengesi primary budget balance

The budget balance calculated with the state's interest payments excluded.

Faiz oranı interest rate

The ratio of the interest to be paid to the borrowed amount.

Faiz riski interest risk

The risk of an unexpected change in the interest rate adversely affecting the value of debts and receivables.

Faizsiz Kredi Desteği

The financial support envisaging that the entirety of the interest or profit-share expenses to be paid in return for the credits to be received from the relevant intermediary institutions is covered by the relevant public institutions and organizations.

Faktoring Factoring

The transaction in which firms engaged in the sale of goods and services for domestic and foreign markets obtain liquid funds in return for transferring the short-term commercial receivable rights that have arisen or will arise from the sale of goods and services. Besides this, the financial institutions providing firms with the opportunity to collect the proceeds of credit sales before their maturity are also called 'factoring' institutions. These firms purchase the invoiced receivables of companies that have made credit sales in cash but at a discount, and collect the receivable themselves when it matures.

Faktör maliyeti factor cost

Or input cost: the cost of the inputs such as labor, capital and land used in the production process.

Faktör piyasası factor market

Or the input market: the markets where the instruments and materials required for production are bought and sold.

FAVÖK EBITDA

Earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation (EBITDA); it shows business performance independent of financing and depreciation policy.

Fayda utility

Or in short U: the conceptual measure showing the satisfaction and benefits a consumer derives from a certain good or service.

Example: Employees receive a post-retirement benefit after retirement.( Employees receive a pension benefit after retirement.

English definition: An advantage or entitlement received under a plan or contract.

utility function utility function

The mathematical relationship showing how total utility changes depending on the quantity consumed.

utility theory utility theory

The body of principles explaining what products a consumer wishing to raise material living quality will consume or can obtain, and in what quantities.

utility maximization utility maximization

The selection of the product bundle that will maximize total utility using a certain budget, with product prices given.

Useful Model

An industrial property right granting the owners of inventions applicable in industry the right to produce and market the product.

surplus surplus

Or excess supply: the situation in which the quantity supplied in the market exceeds the quantity demanded.

Federal Funds Rates Federal Funds Rate

The money market interest rate at which financial institutions in the United States carry out their overnight borrowing. Since it is of the nature of a fundamental indicator in the implementation of monetary policy, it is under the close supervision of the US central bank (FED). With the aim of the daily 'Federal Funds Rates' forming in this market following a course consistent with its announced target rate, the FED adjusts the daily reserve (available funds) amount in the market through open market operations. For example, if the interest rates forming in this market are below the FED's target rate — in other words, if there is a fund surplus in the market — the FED withdraws this amount from the market through open market operations.

Federal Funds Rate Fed Funds Rate

The interest rate applied to the transaction in which banks and other depositary institutions in the United States lend their free reserves in their Fed accounts overnight.

fiat money fiat money

General payment instruments that have no significant concrete use value and gain value and function through laws and state guarantee.

Financial account Financial account

The main heading in the balance of payments showing the changes relating to financial assets and liabilities.

Financial Account - on a Balance of Payments Basis Financial Account - on a Balance of Payments Basis

An account in which the short- and long-term international capital flows carried out by the central bank, general government (central administration, local administrations, social security funds), banks and other sectors (other financial corporations and non-financial corporations, households and non-profit institutions) are recorded; it fundamentally contains the changes in a country's external financial assets and liabilities and the counterpart records of these changes.

Financial independence financial independence

The central bank's having sufficient financial resources to fulfill its targets and being able to determine its own budget.

Financial Contagion Financial Contagion

International investors who are alarmed by problems arising in one or a few countries rapidly withdrawing their investments from countries with similar characteristics, whereby the adverse investment conditions spread also to the financial systems of other countries.

Financial Deepening Financial Deepening

The growth of financial services enabling wider service options to reach every segment of society. It can also be defined as the ratio at which the funds created in the financial sector are transferred to the real sector. The term 'financial deepening' can be used in a different sense in relation to the macro effects it brings to economies. Accordingly, greater financial deepening means an increase in the money supply, and the increase in the money supply brings economic growth along with it.

Financial Education Financial Education

The process in which, through individuals being informed on financial matters, awareness of financial products, opportunities and risks increases, and consumers and investors, learning the ways of accessing financial information, develop the ability to reflect the knowledge and competence they acquire onto their economic behavior and to make conscious financial decisions.

Financial Awareness Financial Awareness

An element that supports persons behaving more rationally in their decision-making processes by increasing their knowledge of, and level of awareness regarding, financial risks.

Financial Accounts Financial Accounts

A set of accounts showing the financial transactions with one another of all the financial assets and liabilities created, converted into cash and transformed in an economy, by sectors and by financial instruments. Taking as its basis the financial transactions domestic sectors carry out with one another and with the rest of the world, it shows how the surplus or deficit in the capital account is financed with financial assets and liabilities. To access the Financial Accounts

Financial Services Survey - FSS Financial Services Survey - FSS

A survey applied monthly with the aim of monitoring the assessments of the recent past and the forward-looking expectations of the managers of financial institutions in Türkiye regarding their business situation, and producing indicators that will reflect the tendencies and developments in the financial services sector. To access the Financial Services Survey

Financial Services Confidence Index - FSCI Financial Services Confidence Index - FSCI

An indicator, with the aim of following the developments in the financial services sector, in which the answers given to different questions of the Financial Services Survey are evaluated together and summarized. Click to access the Financial Services Confidence Index.

access to financial services access to financial services

The concept describing to what extent economic units can easily benefit from banking and insurance services.

financial stability financial stability

The resilience or protection of financial institutions such as banks and stock exchanges in a country against unexpected changes.

Financial Stability Financial Stability

Refers to the stability and resilience against shocks in the financial markets, in the institutions operating in these markets and in the payment systems. Stability in these areas generally brings with it the healthy and stable functioning of the financial system, and hence the productive allocation of the resources in the economy and the appropriate management and distribution of risks. It is a known fact that financial instability, on the other hand, will create serious problems in the economy, and the high cost of the financial crises experienced points to the importance of financial stability.

Financial Stability Committee Financial Stability Committee

The committee established with the change made in Law No. 4059 by Decree-Law No. 637, which entered into force on 8 June 2011, in order to closely and effectively monitor macro financial risks in Türkiye. The Financial Stability Committee, under the chairmanship of the Minister of Treasury and Finance of the Republic of Türkiye, consists of the Governor of the CBRT, the Chairman of the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency, the Chairman of the Capital Markets Board and the President of the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund. Its fundamental duties are to control financial risks by providing coordination among the member institutions and to prevent the formation of systemic risk.

Financial Stability Board Financial Stability Board-FSB

An international organization established in April 2009 as the successor of the Financial Stability Forum, with the aim of coordinating the work of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies, and of developing and implementing effective regulation, supervision and other financial sector policies, for the achievement of financial stability.

Financial leverage Financial leverage

The effect of debt financing on magnifying return on equity; it cuts both ways, since it also enlarges losses in low-profit periods.

Foreign Exchange Assets and Liabilities of Non-Financial Companies Foreign Exchange Assets and Liabilities of Non-Financial Companies

In Türkiye, the difference between the foreign currency assets and foreign currency liabilities of firms operating outside the financial sector arising from their transactions with the domestic financial sector and with residents abroad. It is used as an indicator of how much of the real sector's foreign-currency-linked liabilities it can cover with its foreign-currency or foreign-currency-indexed assets. To access the Non-Financial Sector Firms' Net FX Position

Leasing Leasing

The financing technique used to meet the medium-term funding needs of enterprises. A contract signed between the lessee and the lessor that leaves the ownership of a good selected by the lessee and purchased by the lessor with the lessor, and its use with the lessee.

The equipment was recognised as a finance lease because ownership transferred at the end of the term.( The equipment was recognised as a finance lease because ownership transferred at the end of the term.

English definition: A lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee.

Financial Literacy Financial Literacy

The competence of an individual to possess the fundamental financial knowledge enabling effective and conscious decisions in the process of managing one's personal budget, and, by implementing these decisions, to raise individual and social financial welfare.

Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures - PFMI Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures - PFMI

The standards prepared for financial market infrastructure institutions, contained in the report published in 2012 by the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI), an international standard-setting organization in the field of payments established under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), an international standard-setting organization in the field of securities. Under the said report, financial market infrastructures are payment systems, securities settlement systems, central counterparties, central securities depositories and data repositories.

Financial liberalization financial liberalization

A country's removal of the restrictions on its financial markets and its integration with the outside world in the financial sense.

Firma firm

The institutions that offer to the market the goods and services demanded by society, with the aim of making profit.

Fisher etkisi Fisher effect

The phenomenon of the nominal interest rate coming out higher than the real interest rate because of the inflation expectation.

Fixed Rebates

Rebates in which there is a single rebate target for buyers and, linked to this target, a single rebate rate is applied.

Fiyat price

The payment made in return for a product bought or sold.

Fiyat alıcı price taker

A buyer or seller having no influence whatsoever over the price of a certain product.

Fiyat ayrımcılığı price discrimination

The practice of selling a certain product to different buyers in ways that earn different amounts of profit.

Fiyat endeksi price index

A series of numbers measuring the price average of a certain group of products for different periods.

Örnek: Sözleşme, bir tüketici fiyat endeksine bağlıdır. ( The contract is linked to a consumer price index.)

English definition: Statistical measure tracking changes in prices of goods.

Fiyat esnekliği price elasticity

Or the price elasticity of demand, in short εP: a basic type of elasticity showing by what percentage the quantity demanded of a product decreases as a result of a one percent increase in its price.

Fiyat istikrarı price stability

The prices of products in a country remaining constant over time, or changing at a low and predictable rate.

Price Stability Price Stability

Refers to a low and stable inflation rate, directed toward the long-term fundamental aims of monetary policy (growth and employment), to the extent that it will not be effective in the decision-making processes of economic units.

price restriction price restriction

The market intervention the state implements by determining the lowest or highest price to be paid for a product.

price leadership model price leadership model

The oligopoly model in which a dominant firm sets the price and the other small firms comply with it.

price war price war

Firms acting with the aim of increasing or preserving market share successively cutting prices in response to one another.

price maker price maker

A buyer or seller possessing influence over the price of a certain product.

Price-to-Book - P/B Price-to-Book - P/B

The ratio of market value to book value; below 1 generally indicates low valuation or poor asset quality.

Price-to-Earnings - P/E Price-to-Earnings - P/E

The ratio of the share price to earnings per share; it shows the price an investor pays for 1 lira of earnings and should be compared across sectors.

physical capital physical capital

; They are man-made equipment such as machines, factories, vehicles, buildings used in production.

Example: Physical capital is measured in units of production capacity.( Physical capital is measured in units of production capacity.

"English definition: Capital viewed as the physical productive capacity of an entity."

Physiocracy physiocracy

The school of thought maintaining that wealth is determined by the amount of agricultural land owned, and that at the basis of economic relations lies a natural order.

Fund Fund

Refers to banknotes, coins, book money or electronic money.

Functional income distribution functional income distribution

The income distribution measure showing how total income is distributed among the production factors.

Fund

The capital formation established through the partnerships of qualified investors who invest in the technology- and innovation-oriented ventures of medium-sized enterprises with high growth potential. Entrepreneur: the person or persons who see business opportunities in any field, take the possible risks and commit themselves to the business, and ensure its continuity.

Forfaiting Forfeiting

The purchase by a bank or a financial institution specialized in this field of receivables, particularly those arising from the export of goods and services, that can be collected according to a certain payment plan. It is a financing instrument for long-term and credit-based export-import transactions, generally used for investment goods.

Forum Shopping

The case of undertakings submitting their complaints or notifications to all of the different institutions having jurisdiction on the same matter, or to one of the institutions, seeking to ensure that decisions favorable to the undertaking are taken. Undertakings try to take advantage of the conflicts of jurisdiction among the institutions. Gelire Endeksli Senetler Revenue Indexed Bonds

With the aim of increasing domestic savings, diversifying Government Domestic Debt Securities and broadening the investor base, the first Revenue-Indexed Securities (GES) issue was carried out by the Ministry of Treasury and Finance of the Republic of Türkiye on 28 January 2009. In GES issues, returns are indexed to the revenue shares transferred to the budget from the Türkiye Petrolleri Anonim Ortaklığı (TPAO), which has the status of a State Economic Enterprise, the State Supply Office (DMO), the State Airports Authority (DHMİ) and the General Directorate of Coastal Safety (KIYEM). With Revenue-Indexed Securities, an investment instrument has been created whose return is linked to state revenues. Thanks to the minimum coupon payment guarantee to be applied to the said securities, the investor is protected from being adversely affected by the change in the revenue share. Within this framework, in calculating the payments relating to the returns of the said securities, the total of the quarterly and semi-annual revenue shares transferred to the budget by TPAO, DMO, DHMİ and KIYEM is taken as the basis. If the realized revenue collection exceeds the maximum amounts announced in the budget, payment is made to investors based on the counterparts of the said maximum amounts.

Yield Curve Yield Curve

The graphical expression of the relationship, in any time interval, between the various maturities of an investment instrument and the returns at those maturities. The vertical axis holds return/yield, the horizontal axis the maturities. They are classified as positively sloped (normal) yield curves, negatively sloped (inverted) yield curves, flat yield curves and yield curves expressing high returns at medium maturities (bell shape). The movements of the curve over time — its steepening ('steeping': if a positively sloped curve is in question, the distant part of the curve rising and the near part falling, the slope increasing), its flattening ('flattening': in positively sloped yield curves, the distant part falling, the near part rising, the slope decreasing) and the curve moving up or down without changing its shape ('parallel shift') — are so named. An increase in the curve's slope reflects the expectation that interest rates (inflation) will rise in the long term. A decrease in the slope — in other words, the flattening of a positively sloped yield curve (the near side rising, the distant side falling) — expresses investors, with the expectation that interest rates will fall in the future, turning toward the long term in order to benefit from the current interest rates for longer, and hence, with the increasing demand, the return at that maturity falling; and those demanding funds, with the expectation that the opportunity of borrowing at lower interest rates will arise in the future, preferring the short term, and hence, with the excess supply, the return rising.

Increasing Returns to Scale

Returns to scale can be defined as the effect on efficiency of the change occurring in the scale of production. Increasing returns to scale is the situation in which the undertaking's average cost falls as the quantity produced rises. There are two sources of this fall. The first is internal, stemming from the increase in the undertaking's level of production. The second is external; accordingly, the increase in the quantity of production in the industry affects the prices in the market in a way that will cause the undertaking to change its production decision

İhale Auction

In market economies, one of the methods of allocating various goods and financial values to individuals or institutions. In particular, if the good to be auctioned has no fixed or directly determinable price, or if the seller of the good is unsure about the good's market price, sale by auction eliminates this uncertainty under fully competitive conditions. Auctions can be conducted in different forms. The most common are the multiple-price (Dutch Auction) type auctions in which prices are ordered from largest to smallest, ensuring maximum revenue and minimum cost for the seller. In this auction, the transaction with each participant is made at the price it itself bid. Auctions in which prices are ordered from smallest to largest are called the 'English Auction'. Another auction method is the 'single price' auction. In this auction type, the price at which supply and demand are equated is applied to all the participants winning the auction. In other words, all the transactions are carried out at a single price. Both auction types have advantages and disadvantages relative to one another. In the single price auction, the cost of information gathering is lower and greater participation can be achieved. In the multiple price auction, more intense competition is in question and a lower cost may be in question for the seller. However, all these depend on the structure of the market and the conditions of the day.

İhale kuramı auction theory

resource

self correcting mechanism self correcting mechanism

rent rent

Market

Competition envisages a system in which there is no obstacle whatsoever to entry into the market. In markets where competition is restricted, however, the undertakings controlling the market, in order not to share their privileged position with others, use methods such as advertising and product differentiation to obstruct entry into the market

Market Power

In a fully competitive market, the price of a product equals its marginal cost, and undertakings cannot influence the market price.
